newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - M'bishi Trust to seek foreign partners.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - M'bishi Trust to seek foreign partners.

text.p: Mitsubishi Trust & Banking Corp says it plans to seek greater cooperation with foreign financial institutions in a bid to fortify its fund management in the face of growing competition.
"Mitsubishi Trust would like to promote tie-ups with foreign financial institutions to increase our (global) network," president Toyoshi Nakano told Reuters in a recent interview.
"Those tie-ups should be aimed at strengthening our fund management," Nakano said.
Mitsubishi Trust, with parent assets of 16.85 trillion yen as of end-March 1996, is Japan's biggest trust bank.
Trust banks engage in ordinary banking as well as managing and administering clients' assets.

To combat expected competition stemming from Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms, which aim to deregulate the nation's financial markets by 2001, trust banks must examine their operations and put greater efforts into areas in which they excel, Nakano said.
Mitsubishi Trust has already agreed to cooperate with major banks in China, India, Indonesia and the Philippines, and wants to improve its asset management through the ties, he said.
"While the cooperation is still at early stages such as exchanging information, we would like to build closer relationships," he said.
"The target (of the tie-ups) is to strengthen our asset management ability," Nakano said.

In March, Mitsubishi Trust and AIG Global Investment Corp, a Japanese unit of American International Group Inc (AIG), set up a joint venture which advises Japanese pension funds and institutional investors on investment, and also develops collective investment vehicles.
The joint venture, AIMIC Investment Management Ltd based in Tokyo, will benefit greatly from AIG's global fund management experience, especially in emerging markets, Nakano said.

Nakano said AIMIC, owned 70 percent by AIG and 30 percent by Mitsubishi Trust, had started marketing its first investment trust, which is similar to mutual funds in the United States, through brokerage house Nikko Securities Co Ltd.

Nakano, who is also chairman of the Trust Companies Association of Japan, said that the trust banking industry should try harder to develop attractive financial products which are exclusive to the industry.

Asked about views aired by some analysts that financially weak trust banks might be acquired by large commercial banks, Nakano said the wide range of businesses that trust banks cover could not be easily taken over.
For example, pension fund management requires a large amount of human resources and as well as substantial investment to establish a computer system, he said.
Last month, Mitsubishi Trust revised its parent profit forecast to 75 billion yen for the past fiscal year which ended on March 31, from an earlier estimate of 130 billion yen.
The downward review comes as a result of Mitsubishi Trust's decision to increase disposal of problem loans to 375 billion yen from initial plans of 320 billion yen.
Company results will be announced in late May.
Nakano said that the bank had reduced problem loans to a manageable level by the end of March.
